description: Synthetic labelled cases for scripts/eval_llm_tier.py in which no SUSPICIOUS case has a rule reason: the suspicion has to be read from the names, jurisdiction and amount in the record. Eight CLEAR controls look ambiguous but are legitimate. Labels were fixed before any model saw the cases. All names are invented. rule_reasons are the output of utils.rules.evaluate_row for the transaction fields.

cases.note: Round sum between numbered sibling companies with generic names; there is no trading reason for one shelf company to pay its twin. A reviewer should notice the near-identical numbered names.
A nominee-director company paying a bearer-share holding company hides who owns both ends. A reviewer should notice 'nominee' and 'bearer' in the names; the jurisdiction is not on the rules' lists.
Payment into a jurisdiction under FATF increased monitoring that the rules' high-risk list does not include. A reviewer should notice the jurisdiction even though no rule fired.
Payment into a jurisdiction under FATF increased monitoring and conflict risk that the rules do not list. A reviewer should notice the jurisdiction even though no rule fired.
Round payment from an advisory firm to a serving deputy minister personally: a politically exposed person receiving private funds. A reviewer should notice the PEP title in the beneficiary name.
Consultancy money into the family trust of a regional governor: a PEP behind a trust. A reviewer should notice the PEP title and the trust wrapper.
A round, large credit from a free-zone trading company into a student account, a typical money-mule recruitment pattern. A reviewer should notice the account type does not fit the payer or the size.
A children's sports club spending a round 6,000 on prepaid gift cards, which are easy to move value through. A reviewer should notice the mismatch between account type and activity.
A numbered collection agent paying a crypto ATM operator: collected funds pushed straight out into crypto. A reviewer should notice the collector name and the cash-to-crypto exit.
A high-street florist buying from a bullion refinery has no business reason; goods mismatch is a trade-based laundering sign. A reviewer should notice the sector mismatch.
Pension money sent to a 'recovery' firm, the classic second stage of an investment scam. A reviewer should notice the recovery-service name and the pension source.

A company paying a coin-mixing service, whose only purpose is to break the trail between where crypto comes from and where it goes. A reviewer should notice the mixing service named as beneficiary; it is not on the sanctions list, so no rule fires.

rule_reasons: Value 285,000.00 is at or above the 10,000 reporting threshold.
cases.note: Private buyers paying their conveyancing solicitor's client account for a house purchase, the normal route for a completion. Looks like the ambiguous client-account pattern but has an ordinary payer.

cases.note: A manufacturer funding its monthly payroll run through a payroll bureau. Large, but the payer and payee fit the amount.

cases.note: A housing association completing a purchase of new-build homes from the developer. Large, but the parties and the size fit.
Cross-border invoice from a furniture maker to a component supplier in a low-risk country.

cases.note: A family foundation making a grant to a registered charity. Foundations and round sums look ambiguous, but grant-making is what the payer exists for.
A small company paying a round dividend to its director, whose surname is the company name. Round sum to a person, but the relationship is plain.
A person buying a small amount of crypto through an exchange. Crypto looks ambiguous, but the size and direction are ordinary retail use.
A textile firm paying a fabric trader abroad; the goods match the payer's business.
